stories.title: Hawks struggle to contain Miami at the rim in loss to Heat
stories.summary: The Hawks were unable to keep Miami’s size away from the rim.
stories.detailText: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 28: Giannis Antetokounmpo #7 of the Miami Heat is defended by Dyson Daniels #5 and Onyeka Okongwu #17 of the Atlanta Hawks during the second quarter at State Farm Arena on October 28, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Atlanta Hawks dropped a third consecutive game as they fell to fellow Southeast Division rivals Miami Heat 129-117 on Wednesday evening at State Farm Arena. Nickeil Alexander-Walker scored 23 points, while rookie Kingston Flemings also scored so far career-best of 23 points. For the Heat, Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo scored 24 points apiece with Antetokounmpo adding 18 rebounds. Having lost two games against the Houston Rockets, the Hawks returned to State Farm Arena to face a familiar foe: a Heat side looking for their first victory of the season. Initially, it was a close affair between the two sides, but the Heat began to edge away as the first quarter came to close and established a double-digit lead as the paint points began to mount. In the second quarter, the Hawks made a run to bring the margin down as low as three points before the Heat re-established themselves and their double-digit lead; a half-court heave from Nikola Jovic at the halftime buzzer putting the Heat up by 13 points. The third quarter saw the Hawks, again, trying to mount a comeback before another Miami run stretched their lead to a game-high 18 points before settling at 15 heading into the final frame. The Hawks mounted a run in the fourth quarter, and with seven minutes remaining the lead had been trimmed to four points — plenty of time to take the lead and see the game through with the home-crowd very much onside. However, Miami responded, and restored their 10-point lead and edge away to secure their first win of the season. Postgame, Hawks head coach Quin Snyder acknowledged that the Heat were just better last night, while also commenting on the Hawks not moving the ball as they should have, affecting their offense. “Credit the way they played, they, they beat us,” said Snyder. “They were aggressive on the glass, they did a lot of things and there were times when we responded, but we’ve got to be better. We’ve got to move the ball better, particularly when the team’s aggressive on us on the ball. We have willing passers, but we have to pass. It’s about when you pass, and our ability to get off the ball quicker and get more movement I think will help us offensively. When we’re not connected on the offensive end, it really impacts our team.” The Hawks made multiple runs in this game to cut the lead to single digits but could not sustain it. “Just a little too late, energy-wise,” said Nickeil Alexander-Walker. “We’re showing that we can compete. I think throughout the game, we have to do a better job of consistently competing. There’s times where our compete level drops, and that’s what it was tonight.” I think the Hawks lost this game for three reasons: they got absolutely killed in the paint/at the rim, the Hawks committed a lot of turnovers that could have been avoided, and Atlanta missed too many bunnies at the rim. The main issue last night defensively was defending at the rim: the Heat made 21 baskets at the rim and scored 70 points in the paint. Onyeka Okongwu certainly had his work cut out for him with both Giannis and Adebayo attacking the rim, or Miami operating Adebayo in the high-post, bringing Okongwu away from the rim and leaving the rim largely unprotected…and then there were instances where Okongwu or Jock Landale were close to the rim and it didn’t matter. This lack of rim protection in this game was seen in the early stages, as Andrew Wiggins drives to the rim and scores before the defense can rotate to attempt a block: View Link After a turnover from Kingston Flemings, the Heat come the other way, and from the corner, Pelle Larsson is able to drive by Aaron Wiggins and score at the rim without a challenge: View Link Here, Adebayo throws an entry pass to Giannis, who has Landale at his back, and with the only size the Hawks have at even having a remote chance of slowing him down, Giannis is able to flip the shot home, plus the foul: View Link Again, Adebayo throws the entry pass into Giannis, who gets Landale at his back, uses his size to carve space and finishes at the rim: View Link After a wide miss by Adebayo on the jumper, there is absolutely no size and no chance the Hawks can prevent Giannis claiming the offensive rebound and scoring at the rim: View Link After the drive from Klay Thompson draws Okongwu, Giannis receives the dump-off at the dunker’s spot, and with Okongwu now behind the play, Giannis can dunk at the rim for another basket at the rim: View Link After Dyson Daniels does a good job contesting the much larger Adebayo at the rim, he — and the rest of the Hawks — are powerless to fight against the second effort of Adebayo, who claims and rises in a crowd to score at the rim: View Link On this drive from Antetokounmpo, Okongwu provides little resistance (hesitating on the drive) and it allows an easy basket at the rim: View Link This time in a rare pick-and-roll scenario, Antetokounmpo gets a head of steam, and when he does it’s just one of those things that’s very difficult to stop even with sufficient rim protection: View Link In a more open-court scenario, Okongwu again doesn’t do enough to track the threat going to the rim and Mitchell scores an easy basket: View Link It’s a tough matchup for the Hawks when there’s an old-school tandem of a dominant power forward/center combo, and the Hawks just don’t have the size to combat this dual-headed threat. “Obviously Giannis and the question before about Bam breaking the rebounding record for the Heat, so, he’s out there and then Giannis is out there too and Portis is physical and they have size across their front line,” said Snyder. “We can’t accept that those aren’t plays and balls that we can come up with. There’s just another level there, and at times we found it. But there are things, that throughout the possession when you have breakdowns, it becomes difficult to rebound because you’re in a rotation situation.” It was undoubtedly the key to the game, but with the way the Hawks are set up I’m not sure what more could have been done to prevent it. Sure, perhaps Okongwu could have gotten back to the rim quicker on some drives to try and contest, but there’s no guarantee that would have changed the outcome on those baskets and, overall, those instances were far fewer than the Heat just inherently having a size advantage possession after possession. Individually, the Hawks did not enjoy many strong offensive performances, in particular Jalen Johnson did not enjoy a positive game scoring the ball, scoring just 12 points on 4-of-12 shooting. Snyder believed the Heat trapping as they did impacted the Hawks and their ability to move the ball as they normally would. “The impact that Jalen has in the game in transition and his unselfishness, his willingness to pass the ball, playing without the ball is something that our, our whole team, the more we embrace that, the more difficult we are to defend, and that’s everybody,” began Snyder on Johnson’s difficult game. “Tonight, they were trapping us in lots of actions, so those reads really dictate that you need to throw the ball ahead and just move it and see how you break the defense down. That’s one of the biggest things for us is to have the ball change sides. When we’re playing actions, that allows them to double, and when they do, we’ve got to take advantage of that. That’s something we need to do a better job.” Johnson was still able to rack up 11 assists, and the Hawks 35 assists but it was the 15 turnovers which were costly for the Hawks. Not so much because Miami punished them for it (only scoring 13 points off of turnovers) but they were largely avoidable turnovers which prevented the Hawks themselves attempting shots. The story from the Hawks’ side from a player perspective was that of Kingston Flemings, who scored 23 points on 9-of-12 shooting from the field and 3-of-5 from three: “Just staying aggressive,” said Flemings of his night. “We got a lot of rebounds, and we were pushing in transition, that’s when we’re best. So, just trying to get rebounds, push and just playing the flow of the offense.” Flemings also got the nod to close out the game in place of CJ McCollum down the stretch, running with the Hawks’ crunch time lineup. When asked about this decision after the game, Snyder explained the reasoning for it and how McCollum has supported Flemings. “Kingston did a terrific job,” said Snyder of Flemings. “I think this is part of the process for him. This is a long runway, as I’ve said and it’s not about any one player, it’s really not. Tonight, Kingston gave us a lift. He was pushing the ball and made some good things happen. We talked about it as the coaching staff, (and) CJ knows how we feel about him, he’s crucial to us being who we want to be. Kingston had been in the game long enough that it felt like throwing CJ in a tough situation, putting him in cold at that point. As I said, CJ’s all about the team and the team winning and that’s an aberration. But I think CJ more than anyone understands with his professionalism and his career, but our whole team, that’s part of having depth on any given night. Hopefully you have guys that can lift their level, and tonight was Kingston. It’s been other guys as well. That’s how we can be a good team by having that depth and versatility and guys getting behind one another. You saw that tonight. Nobody’s more supportive of Kingston than CJ.” Flemings echoed this sentiment and described how McCollum has been helping him in his rookie season so far. “I mean, otherworldly, to be honest,” said Flemings when asked about the importance of McCollum’s veteran presence. “Him and Nickeil, I work out with them almost every single day, taking bits and pieces. For CJ to be playing this long at this high of a level, it’s not easy to do. You don’t even see a lot of players doing it. But just CJ, the things he’s done, he’s in my ear all the time. Every timeout when he’s on the bench, just telling me what he sees, offense, defense, helping me in those ways. Just invaluable having players like him on the team. I’m grateful for it.” “I just work with him every day, so, seeing his mindset, seeing his aggression, the way he competed tonight was amazing,” added Nickeil Alexander-Walker of Flemings. “He provided energy, came in aggressive, played to his strengths, got the team within striking distance in multiple ways. His force and everything was amazing.” In some of those plays from his highlights above, what continues to be really impressive is Flemings’ decision-making. He could spring into a three or a jumpshot, but turns it down and drives inside, where he can either kick it out or rise into a more open jumpshot. It would be easy to take the three in front of him but takes maturity to recognize that there is a better shot available to him; his patience has been impressive to watch. “The game is still super fast,” said Flemings postgame. “I think it’s definitely slowing down for me. It’s just being aggressive. I see a lot of the plays throughout the court, nothing really changed. It’s just when the defense knows I’m going to pass, my passes aren’t going to be there. So, the coaches talk to me about that, everyone’s talking about that. Putting the ball on the rim, I’m going to continue to do that. Just put the ball up, make some shots, and you play like that, it makes the defense second guess. So, doing that, just constantly trying to gain confidence throughout.” Other Hawks who had a good game include Dyson Daniels, he was so disruptive defensively last night — three steals doesn’t fully reflect how active he was last night. Alexander-Walker scored 23 points on 8-of-18 from the field and 5-of-9 from three, while CJ McCollum was active in the first quarter and made some tough baskets en route to 13 points. Despite Johnson shooting 4-of-12, Lu Dort shooting 3-of-11, and Aaron Wiggins shooting 4-of-11, I thought the offense wasn’t really the issue (barring those turnovers); the Hawks just had no answer to Miami’s size — the roster is just fundamentally built in a way that does not jive well with the way Atlanta’s roster is built. The Hawks have now lost three straight games, but this doesn’t require overreaction. Two of those are against the Rockets, and they’re just a step above the Hawks from a talent perspective: that’s going to be a very good team if health endures. This loss last night I think is just a clash of styles that doesn’t suit Atlanta; the Heat’s front court was just too big and powerful for the Hawks to handle last night. Future matchups will be interesting to see how the Hawks go about teams like this with two prolific bigs. The Hawks (2-3) are back in action tonight at State Farm Arena to take on the Cleveland Cavaliers (3-1), who were in action last night in a win against the Wizards in Cleveland. Until next time!

stories.title: Heard ‘em Say: Bucks turned down picks for KPJ, Wisconsin Herd roster roundup, Jaylen Brown, and more!
stories.summary: Tidbits from the Milwaukee Bucks universe.
stories.detailText: MILWAUKEE, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 05: Kevin Porter Jr. #7 of the Milwaukee Bucks looks on against the Minnesota Timberwolves during the preseason NBA game at Fiserv Forum on October 05, 2026 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to another edition of Heard ‘em Say, where we share the Milwaukee Bucks news that matters to you—all in one convenient place! On this week’s agenda: what could have been instead of waiving Kevin Porter Jr., a roundup of the Wisconsin Herd’s roster, an update on Malik Beasley’s sports gambling charges, and Nate Ament reps the Brewers. Oh, and was Jaylen Brown pushing to become a Buck? Nuggets offered picks for KPJ? As you’re well aware, the Bucks waived Kevin Porter Jr. just before the 4:00 p.m. CT deadline for NBA teams to finalise their rosters ahead of the regular season starting. The news was a shock, at least to some ( Editor’s note: more on that to come ), particular given how well Porter performed when healthy last season. As it turns out, the Bucks didn’t have to lose him for nothing. In fact, according to Jake Fischer’s report in The People’s Insider , they could’ve received draft picks in exchange for the 26-year-old. Of course, there’s a caveat: The Stein Line has learned that the Nuggets showed a willingness to package two future second-rounders and a second-round pick swap along with Zeke Nnaji’s very available contract in a bid to bring Kevin Porter Jr. to the Rocky Mountains. Yet I’m told that the Bucks ultimately walked away from the Porter-to-Denver discussions as well — and then waived Porter Jr. — because they could not stomach the idea of swallowing Nnaji’s $7.5 million salary for the 2027-28 season. Fischer also reported that five salary cap specialists from rival teams “said they would have made the move if they were in Milwaukee’s shoes” but also that “All five capologists say they could understand why the Bucks ultimately chose not to surrender $7.5 million of their theoretical flexibility entering the 2027-28 campaign.” All this considered—not to mention the additional opportunities Porter’s absence has afforded Kasparas Jakučionis—do you agree with Jon Horst’s decision? Speaking of Porter, via the Clutch Scoops podcast , ClutchPoints’ Brett Siegel speculated that while a return to the NBA isn’t out of the cards, Porter may even head back to Europe: Halfway through the year, there’s going to be teams needing point guards and needing more backcourt depth. They’ll look at Kevin Porter Jr. as an option. But I would just keep an eye on him as also being an option for international teams overseas in Europe. And I expect him to gain interest there. We’ll see what he ultimately decides, whether he wants to give up on the NBA and go overseas or if he’s going to wait for some of these pro-rated deals after the trade deadline. As we know, Porter has more than enough talent for NBA basketball, and if it weren’t for all his injuries last year he could very well be the Bucks’ starting point guard right now . So, let’s hope he gets another shot somewhere. All the best, Scoot. Wisconsin Herd roster roundup After making their pick in the G League Draft last Saturday, the Wisconsin Herd have officially finalized their 15-man training camp roster. The roster is led by two-way players Kam Jones, Pete Nance, and Cormac Ryan. Despite trading a 2026 first-rounder to the Capital City Go-Go (the Wizards’ G League affiliate), the Herd still walked away with a player after the draft. The Herd selected Brody Fox, a former The Citadel forward coming off a one-year stint in Estonia, with the 49th pick. Some of the Herd’s most recognizable players parted ways with Wisconsin earlier this year. Mark Sears (19.1 ppg) signed an Exhibit-10 deal with Portland, while Wisconsin traded Stephen Thompson (17.4 ppg) to the Iowa Wolves, and Johnny Davis (15.6 ppg) signed with a Turkish team. The Herd went 10-26 last year, good for last in the Eastern Conference, but coach Schuyler Rimmer and the Herd are hoping to improve going into 2027. The full roster is as follows: Ty Berry (guard, Kauhajoki Karhu) Johni Broome (forward, Philadelphia 76ers/Delaware Blue Coats) Jeremiah Burke (forward, Denver University) John Butler Jr. (forward, Wisconsin Herd) Brody Fox (forward, Latvijas Universitate) Marcus Garrett (guard, Greensboro Swarm) Terrence Hargrove Jr. (forward, Grand Rapids Gold) Kam Jones (guard, Indiana Pacers/Noblesville Boom) Cameron Martin (forward, Wisconsin Herd) Pete Nance (forward, Milwaukee Bucks/Wisconsin Herd) Manny Obaseki (guard, Westchester Knicks) Cameron Parker (guard, Rip City Remix) Cormac Ryan (guard, Milwaukee Bucks/Wisconsin Herd) Kalifa Sakho (forward, Houston University) Jake Stephens (forward, KK Split) Malik Beasley in talks over possible guilty plea In June 2025, news broke that former Bucks guard Malik Beasley was under investigation for betting on NBA games. This June, Beasley was indicted on sports gambling charges , allegedly committing those crimes while with the team. Now, it appears Beasley is pleading guilty, as reported by Mike Vorkunov from The Athletic: Beasley was indicted this summer for his role in an alleged scheme that bet on his performance while he was with the Milwaukee Bucks during the 2023-24 season. Beasley is accused of manipulating his play so that bettors could win their wagers on him. Beasley initially pleaded not guilty, but court records Friday night said that he intends to change his plea. Steve Haney, a lawyer for Beasley, said Beasley has not yet decided to plead guilty, but is in talks with prosecutors with the US Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of New York. He is expected to make a final decision early next week. In fact, there’s no doubt about it: Former NBA player Malik Beasley will enter a guilty plea on Dec. 9 with the Department of Justice over his role in bribery and betting scheme on his NBA play, his attorney Steve Haney tells ESPN. — Shams Charania (@ShamsCharania) October 27, 2026 Yikes. Jaylen Brown may or may not have pushed to be traded to Milwaukee According to Brian Scalabrine, at one point this offseason, Jaylen Brown pushed to be traded to the Milwaukee Bucks: “My understanding is that Jaylen Brown went to the organization and had a list of demands, and it was like, ‘You either do this, or you trade me.’ And he was rooting to get traded to Milwaukee, including calling some teammates about, ‘Hey, man, what do you think of Milwaukee? We should go there.'” Then again, according to the same Brian Scalabrine, that actually didn’t happen: Drew Carter and Brian Scalabrine taking about Scal’s comments on the radio today https://t.co/Ldad81lQHO — Ian Inangelo (@iinangelo) October 26, 2026 For as good as Brown is, I’m good with how this all played out. What about you? Nate Ament & the “Brew Crew” Finally, just in case you missed it, Nate Ament is embracing all things Milwaukee—even with his shoes: Bucks rookie Nate Ament is debuting his “Brew Crew” Reebok Engine A 26 PE today — as the Milwaukee Brewers begin the World Series. The 1-of-1 PE features his player logo on the tongue and a classic navy / yellow Brewers colorway. https://t.co/xGRnvCu5BX — Nick DePaula (@NickDePaula) October 23, 2026 Way to go, Nate. And way to go Brewers! For more on your World Series champion Brewers, be sure to head on over to our friends at Brew Crew Ball . That’s it for this edition, folks. Got any Bucks news or rumours? If so, share them in the comments—or perhaps even as an extended post in The Feed .

stories.summary: Washington Wizards rookie AJ Dybantsa made an immediate impact in his NBA debut, scoring 19 points against the Cleveland Cavaliers (3-1) after missing the first four games of the season with a sprained ankle that he suffered in preseason. The No. 1 overall pick earned a spot in the starting lineup alongside Trae Young…
stories.detailText: CLEVELAND, OH - OCTOBER 28: AJ Dybantsa #4 of the Washington Wizards handles the ball during the game against the Cleveland Cavaliers on October 28, 2026 at Rocket Arena in Cleveland, Ohio. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Brian Kolin/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images Washington Wizards rookie AJ Dybantsa made an immediate impact in his NBA debut, scoring 19 points against the Cleveland Cavaliers (3-1) after missing the first four games of the season with a sprained ankle that he suffered in preseason. The No. 1 overall pick earned a spot in the starting lineup alongside Trae Young, Anthony Davis, Alex Sarr and Kyshawn George as Washington (2-3) shifted fourth-year wing Bilal Coulibaly to come off the bench for the first time this season. Playing on a minutes restriction due to his injury, Dybantsa wasted little time making his presence felt. After Washington won the opening tip, it took Dybantsa just 16 seconds to attack the rim and draw a shooting foul on Cavaliers center Jarrett Allen to send the rookie to the charity stripe. The BYU product knocked down both free throws for the first two points of his NBA career. In his first six-minute stint as a pro, Dybantsa scored nine points on 3-for-3 shooting in the first quarter. He caught a half-court lob from Young, connected on his first career 3-pointer and recorded an assist to Sarr for a corner three in an impressive opening stretch. AJ Dybantsa's FIRST BUCKET IN HIS NBA DEBUT was a lob from Trae 🔥 (via NBA) pic.twitter.com/WV8TP3cFES — Basketball Forever (@bballforever_) October 28, 2026 He exited the first quarter helping Washington take a 22-16 lead, and turned heads with a dazzling step through floater finish, past James Harden and over the seven-footer — Allen. AJ DYBANTSA STEP-THROUGH BUCKET THROUGH THREE DEFENDERS 😱🔥 pic.twitter.com/aFjQfyI4jk — WizardsMuse (@WizardsMuse1) October 28, 2026 Despite the minutes restriction, Dybantsa played the final 8 minutes and 18 seconds of the fourth quarter, with Washington trailing 102-99. He connected on a mid-range jumper and a dunk as Washington — which led by 16 at one point — tried to re-take its lead in the final quarter. The rookie finished with 19 points on 8-for-12 shooting from the field, adding two rebounds and two assists in 27 minutes. But, despite Dybantsa’s strong debut, Cleveland took control late in the game to secure the 121-111 victory over Washington — handing the Wizards their second consecutive loss of the season. Dybantsa’s 19-point performance marked the highest-scoring debut by a Wizards rookie since Tom Gugliotta scored 20 points against the Charlotte Hornets on Nov. 2, 1992. Although Washington couldn’t come away with a win, Dybantsa’s efficient scoring and early contributions offered an encouraging glimpse of what the franchise’s top pick could bring as he begins his NBA career. He will be back in action for his home crowd debut at Capital One Arena against the Charlotte Hornets on Friday night at 7 p.m. ET. Charlotte beat Washington 110-103 on Monday night in North Carolina – while Dybantsa was sidelined.

stories.title: Yaxel Lendeborg ‘amazed' by Steph Curry's big night in win over Timberwolves
stories.summary: After Golden State Warriors star Steph Curry scored 44 points, Yaxel Lendeborg expressed his amazement after the win over the Timberwolves
stories.detailText: Yaxel Lendeborg ‘amazed' by Steph Curry's big night in win over Timberwolves originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area The Warriors won their second straight game, defeating the Minnesota Timberwolves 119-114 in a close final quarter, as Golden State rookie Yaxel Lendeborg continued his early season success. But it was star Steph Curry that put on a show, scoring 44 points on six 3-pointers and still showing that he is critical to Golden State’s core. Lendeborg spoke to reporters after the game and expressed his amazement at Curry’s performance, while acknowledging that it motivated him to do his part for the team. “I think I need somebody to cuss me out, like Draymond [Green] did today, because I’m just watching, like, man, this guy is good as hell,” Lendeborg said. “I caught myself shaking my head, like ‘wow,’ a couple times. But once he got out of the game, it’s like, this is my opportunity to help him out, help his great [game] be worth a lot. But I was amazed today for sure.” Curry scored 19 points in the second quarter in about nine minutes, putting Golden State ahead by a considerable amount going into the second half. But it was the second half that really turned heads, with Curry scoring 21 points and going 16 for 16 at the free throw line for the night. Lendeborg, who was one of only three Warriors, including Curry, to score in double figures, had seven turnovers, but Curry’s big game made those turnovers less important to the outcome of the game. The Warriors are severely shorthanded to start the season , with Jimmy Butler, Moses Moody and Kristaps Porziņģis all sidelined with injuries. Butler and Moody are not expected back until the start of the next calendar year, making Lendeborg’s presence even more important. The rookie is averaging 22.6 points, 9.2 rebounds and 4.0 assists through the first five games, proving that he and Curry form a strong duo. Golden State gets a night off on Thursday before beginning their NBA Cup campaign on Friday night against the Los Angeles Lakers at home. Lendeborg scored 12 points in a 127-105 loss to the Lakers on opening night, and is hoping to improve on that performance and lead the team to a win over their rivals this time around. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Jessie Alcheh/Getty Images) | Getty Images It was always going to be that way, just like Ewings_Finger_Roll joked in the Postgame Thread . There seemed to be nothing the New York Knicks could have done in last night’s road game against the lowly Chicago Bulls that would have made many in their fanbase jump out of their wonderful plushy seats from which they watched a championship just half a year ago. But man, Jordan Clarkson and his friends surely tried nonetheless. To make things a little interesting, the reigning champs went by the playbook of last year’s early-season game at Chicago on October 31, 2025, even if that Cup contest wasn’t on the second night of a back-to-back like this one. They still sleepwalked through it against a young, inexperienced outfit of bull calves which bears no resemblance to the mighty teams of the Windy City’s past—let me know if that sounds familiar. Then, in the end, your Knickerbockers made a furious comeback only to have it fall short just before the finish line. When Norman Powell put Chicago up by 19 midway through the third quarter, that looked like it would be a good bet to happen again. I’m sure you could have found a parlay or something with one of the many bloodthirsty gambling companies that populate our sports world these days. But as is so often the case, that money would have been gone. Knicks play around and still win Would it have been nice if the Knicks hadn’t played with their food so much but rather gulped it down immediately, just like my young Labrador does with anything edible (and not edible) that gets within a mile of his jaws? I’d guess so. Letting a young and, in parts, actually talented team like the Bulls gain confidence is a dangerous proposition. It can quickly turn a game into a mess that it just shouldn’t be, not even on the second night of a back-to-back. It can get players benched, too, as Mikal Bridges can confirm after getting just 13 minutes in this one. But while there are plenty of gripes to be had about how the first two and a half quarters went this time around, nobody can argue with the final result. Josh Hart interrupts Benny The Bull’s dark magic ritual and squares up on him pic.twitter.com/kqNfLt93Jo — KNICKS BEAST (@KnicksBeast) October 29, 2026 In large part, we can thank the Knicks reserves for that, especially Jordan Clarkson, Landry Shamet and Tyler Kolek. They all took turns scoring, defending, passing and fighting; their energy, especially on the offensive end, was palpable. With better and, most notably, quicker ball movement initiated by Kolek (9 assists) came more and more open opportunities from downtown, and the Knicks capitalized (48 percent from three). What a game like this means for Kolek going forward is hard to say, especially once Jose Alvarado comes back from his injury. But even with a more than crowded backcourt, there is probably always room for classy, heads-up point guard play. Jalen Brunson’s wrist looked pretty solid It’s not really how Jalen Brunson interprets his role at the one, but we’ll take the alternative for now. The captain was his vintage self in his former home state, going for 38 big points in a game where his team needed each one of them. Fourteen of those came in the fourth quarter, when there was nothing the Bulls could do to stop the reigning Finals MVP. Word on the street is that Norman Powell is still looking for his ankles around the United Center; considering how he is an old buddy of OG Anunoby from their Toronto days, we surely wish him the best. The most welcome sign from Brunson’s game was that he finally had his three-pointer going (6 of 10 from beyond the arc). Wrist surgeries can be a tricky thing for shooters, and quite a few people were at least slightly concerned when Brunson started the season ice cold from the floor. Worry no more, my friends: our captain is still our captain, and the wrist looked fine. Just like the Knicks did in the end when they pulled out a game that easily could have been one of those dreaded schedule losses that we’ve luckily grown accustomed to over the last few years. I mention “luckily” because you basically can only have these types of losses when you are a good team. When people expect you to win, when they expect you to walk over the bottom feeders of the Association. There’s a temptation to chalk these games up as business as usual no matter the result, especially if you’ve partied up and down the Canyon of Heroes in June. But winning them more often than not points to a certain quality a team possesses. And witnessing that never gets boring, does it?

stories.title: Miles Bridges must improve quickly to justify the Suns’ trade
stories.summary: Miles Bridges has underperformed in his short time as Sun. How short is his leash before we declare it a disaster?
stories.detailText: The Phoenix Suns are last in the NBA in defensive rating early in the 2026-27 season, and their offense over three games has not been anything to celebrate either. You can point the finger at a lot of different people as to why this season has started slowly, and that there are too many fatal flaws on this roster to overcome. Devin Booker, Brian Gregory, Mat Ishbia, and injuries at center all share some level of blame, but it is Miles Bridges who sits at -17.0 in net rating this season, only trailing Booker with a -17.7 net rating on the Suns. When Bridges was brought in this offseason, the hope was for him to be a 6’8” version of Jordan Goodwin in the starting lineup. A guy who plays with an elite motor, defends and rebounds at an elite level, and is capable of knocking down open threes. That has not materialized early on defense at all, while the rebounding has been fine at 6.3 per game, but not where it needs to be for this Suns team to win. The entire team shares the blame for their inability to rebound and defend on the defensive end this season, but Bridges’ athleticism was supposed to give that group a boost, and instead, it’s dragged them down to the bottom. Because of the injuries to Oso Ighodaro and Mark Williams, Bridges has been called upon to be a small-ball center, which has not gone smoothly for anyone, especially Bridges. ‘Offensively, it has gone as poorly as anyone could have imagined so far for the Suns this season, with no Suns starter shooting above 33% from three. Bridges is the worst shooter on the Suns right now; he is taking 6.7 long-distance attempts (second on the team) and connecting on only 20% of them. Many of those attempts are late into the shot clock, heaves that have even less of a chance at going in. The hope for Bridges this season was that he could at least make teams pay when opposing teams left him wide open, but that has backfired. It would be easy for us as a Suns community to declare this trade a catastrophic failure. We gave up Royce O’Neale and Grayson Allen, plus an unprotected first-round pick, for someone playing this poorly. And if this trend continues from Bridges, Mat Ishbia and Brian Gregory’s management of this roster has to be examined under the microscope because it has Bradley Beal levels of stink to it right now. But before I make any certain claims about this trade, we should give the Suns more time. Bridges is one of three new rotation players on this roster, and he missed a significant portion of the preseason with an ankle sprain. It has only been three games, and a week of good shooting and better defense from Bridges will turn his season around in a hurry. He is a better player, or at least has been a better player than what he has shown so far, but the level of patience for him to figure things out is dwindling fast because of the price the Suns paid to get him, on top of the off-the-floor issues he has to overcome to be accepted by Suns fans. The nonnegotiable for Bridges to win Suns fans over and help the team win is that he has to play with incredible effort. He has to be the spark plug for the starting unit as the guy who creates extra possessions for the Suns and sets the tone with toughness and physicality. If he brings that consistently, the Suns can work through the rest of their mess and survive if he fills that role this starting unit desperately needs. On top of the motivation to win games, Bridges is also playing for a contract extension this season and is in prove-it mode on a new team, so there are no excuses for not getting his best effort on a nightly basis. However, if Bridges and the Suns’ play does not improve before the calendar turns to December, then this season, which is quickly spiraling out of control, is only going to get messier, and Bridges’ time in the Valley will be extremely short. That would be another F on Mat Ishbia’s report card during his short time as owner of the Phoenix Suns.

stories.title: Lakers’ hot start couldn’t hide glaring weakness, and it was just exposed
stories.summary: The Lakers' 3-0 start masked glaring defensive flaws. After allowing 136 points to Portland, can Luka Doncic and Walker Kessler overcome LA's biggest weakness?
stories.detailText: That didn’t last long. For three glorious games, the Lakers looked like they had discovered the secret to winning basketball in 2026: score so many points on offense that nobody notices you can’t stop anybody on defense. Through their first three games of the NBA season, Luka Doncic was putting up MVP numbers. Austin Reaves was playing like an All-Star and the perfect No. 2 scoring option alongside Doncic. Walker Kessler looked like the trade of the century, catching alley-oops, protecting the rim and putting up numbers at center the Lakers haven’t seen since Wilt Chamberlain and Shaquille O’Neal. Damian Lillard (0) of the Portland Trail Blazers shoots a 3-point basket during a game against the Los Angeles Lakers at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles, Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images Then the Trail Blazers came to town Tuesday night and delivered a 136-129 reality check that exposed the same glaring weakness everyone worried about before the season began. The Lakers still can’t defend the perimeter, and no amount of offensive fireworks can hide that fact forever. Portland shot a ridiculous 59% from the field, buried 18 of 36 3-pointers and scored at least 32 points in every quarter. The Blazers didn’t just exploit the Lakers’ defense, they made them look like traffic cones on the court during a shootaround. “We got broken down a lot,” Lakers coach JJ Redick admitted afterward. “The game-plan discipline, KYP [Know Your Personnel] discipline wasn’t where it needs to be.” Ja Morant repeatedly sliced through Los Angeles’ perimeter defenders, forcing help rotations that left shooters open. Deni Avdija scored at will, including behind the arc for 23 points. Jrue Holiday added 22. Damian Lillard reminded everyone in attendance at Crypto.com Arena that “Dame Time” is still alive and well, delivering dagger after dagger in the fourth quarter, including the game-clinching basket with 43 seconds remaining. Portland Trail Blazers forward Deni Avdija (8) reacts after scoring a three-pointer during the second half of an NBA basketball game against the Los Angeles Lakers, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, in Los Angeles. AP Photo/Caroline Brehman Frankly, the Lakers had no answers for the Trail Blazers’ offense. And that should concern Redick considerably more than his team’s first loss. Through four games, Los Angeles averaged 128.2 points, second in the NBA, with an offensive rating of 126.8. But its defensive rating of 118.8 ranks 23rd. Those numbers tell the story of a team capable of winning 50 games while possessing the same defensive vulnerability that could send them home early in the playoffs for the fourth straight year. Ja Morant #1 and Damian Lillard #0 of the Portland Trail Blazers celebrate a Lillard three pointer during a 136-129 Blazers win over the Los Angeles Lakers at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Getty Images Make no mistake, these Lakers are going to win plenty of basketball games this season. Assuming reasonable health, another 50-win season and a top-four seed in the Western Conference is entirely realistic. But there’s a drastic difference between being an entertaining team throughout the season and being an actual threat to compete for a championship. Doncic scored 41 points against Portland, following his spectacular 52-point performance in Utah. Reaves contributed 26. Yet the Lakers still lost because their opponents were getting whatever shots they wanted. “We had a lot of blown assignments. It was everybody, it wasn’t just one person,” Reaves said. “I made some bad defensive mistakes. You could go around the room. So, [we] gotta be better.” You cannot ask Doncic to score 40 every night just to compensate for teammates who cannot stay in front of their assignments. Last season, Redick did his best with the roster he had by increasing energy and effort and switching to a zone defense at various points during the year. Honestly, it was amazing the Lakers won their first-round matchup in the playoffs with the Rockets considering their defensive inefficiencies and being without Doncic and Reaves. This season, the problem isn’t effort alone. It’s once again about personnel. Austin Reaves (15) of the Los Angeles Lakers and Ja Morant (1) of the Portland Trail Blazers smile during a game at Crypto.Com Arena in Los Angeles, Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images The Lakers lack sufficient lateral quickness along the perimeter. When opposing guards penetrate, defenders collapse, rotations become scrambled and shooters find themselves with enough daylight to start a vegetable garden. That leaves Kessler cleaning up everyone else’s mess. The 7-footer has been outstanding, but he’s being asked to protect the rim, contest drives, cover defensive breakdowns and somehow recover quickly enough to secure rebounds. Even the best defensive centers cannot be in two places on the court simultaneously. “We were breaking down and giving up corner 3s, pull-to-break 3s,” Kessler said. “I pride myself on being the leader on the defense, and I didn’t perform tonight.” And the Lakers have another problem when it comes to Kessler: Who replaces him when he comes out of the game for a much-needed rest? Kevon Looney has struggled to provide dependable minutes , leaving Los Angeles dangerously thin behind Kessler. For a center with an injury history, carrying this much defensive responsibility over 82 games is asking for trouble. Rob Pelinka should already be exploring the trade market for a legitimate backup center rather than waiting until Kessler’s workload becomes a medical concern. Redick deserves credit for experimenting with defensive schemes, including zone looks last season, but coaching adjustments cannot manufacture foot speed. First-round pick Cameron Carr, once healthy, possesses the youth, athleticism and defensive potential that this roster desperately needs. The Baylor product won’t magically solve everything, but he deserves an opportunity to demonstrate whether he can defend NBA guards without requiring three teammates to rescue him. The Lakers don’t need another scorer. They need somebody who takes pride in preventing one. Redick said it best after Tuesday’s loss. “If we score 129 points at home, we should be able to get enough stops to win.” He’s right. Los Angeles can score with anybody in the NBA. The question is whether it can stop anybody when it matters most. stories.title: Clippers continue to struggle with turnovers to start 2026-27 season
stories.summary: The Los Angeles Clippers continue to struggle with turnovers to start the season. Here's what the team is saying about the issue.
stories.detailText: INGLEWOOD, CA — Darius Garland and the Los Angeles Clippers continue to struggle with turnovers to start the season. The turnovers happened early and often for the Clippers, who fell to 1-3 on the season after losing to the Lakers on Wednesday, Oct. 28. Isaiah Jackson won the tip-off against Lakers center Walker Kessler to start the game, but Garland was caught off guard and didn't recover the ball as he was still tying his hair while the ball rolled out of bounds. Garland was responsible for five of the team's 24 turnovers on Wednesday. Rookie Keaton Wagler was one of four players to have three turnovers. Coach Tyronn Lue expressed the importance of his team taking care of the ball before the game, but that didn’t come to fruition. The Lakers managed to capitalize on these turnovers and scored 31 points. The Clippers are also the first team since 2002 to have recorded three consecutive games with 24+ turnovers. The Lakers managed to produce a 17-0 scoring run in the second quarter and outscored the Clippers 26-6 on fastbreak points, but Lue directed that result to the turnovers. “I wouldn’t say fastbreak, I'd say turnovers that led to easy 3-on-1s or 1-on-0,” Lue said. “As far as transition, I don't think we did a bad job with that; I think our transition hurt us when we turn the ball over because nobody can get back when that happens.” With Luka Dončić out, the Clippers managed to limit the Lakers' best available scoring option, Austin Reaves, with their defense. Reaves was 6-of-16 from the field and finished with 16 points and six rebounds while turning the ball over eight times. "I think over the four games defensively we've done a lot of good things and we are causing turnovers, but we are just giving it back,” Clippers guard Kris Dunn said. “If we can execute when we do cause turnovers or when we are in the half-court offense and execute, we give ourselves more than a great chance to win these ball games. ... If we can cut down the turnovers, what could the record look like?" When do Clippers play next? The Clippers can snap their three-game losing streak with a road win against the Minnesota Timberwolves on Friday, Oct. 30. teamStories.title: Debunk or double down? Judging 10 early-season NBA overreactions
teamStories.summary: A 29-year-old is the NBA's next breakout star. Miami's Giannis era is already cooked. And so are the Thunder, Knicks and Warriors. Which overreactions are valid?
teamStories.detailText: Welcome to the final days of October, featuring falling leaves, early sunsets, Halloween decorations illuminating the night -- and the yearly pastime of overreacting to the first week of a new NBA season . After all, small sample size theatre has provided early gems such as: The sky is falling in Oklahoma City , New York and Miami ! The three-guard experiment in San Antonio needs to go! Charlotte is already better without LaMelo Ball ! Ty Jerome ? Ty Jerome! With those early storylines and more in mind, let's examine 10 popular overreactions to the young 2026-27 season -- and determine which have staying power. ( Note: stats through Tuesday's games .) The Miami Heat will finish with their worst record since 2008. Zach Kram: Not an overreaction For reference, 2007-08 was the last time the Heat finished with fewer than 37 wins, the season that they tanked down the stretch to go 15-67 in a futile attempt to land Derrick Rose in the draft. Merely by the law of averages, the 2026-27 Heat are bound to improve. They've had the seventh-worst shooting luck on offense, according to GeniusIQ tracking, and the second-worst shooting luck on defense. Miami is actually forcing teams into tough shots, but its opponents have been on fire regardless, making 53% of their midrange shots and 40% of their 3s, per Cleaning the Glass. On the other hand, the Heat's offense has been stuck in the mud even accounting for that poor shooting luck, and guard Davion Mitchell is the only role player who looks comfortable playing with Giannis Antetokounmpo . There's time for that to change -- but as of Wednesday, ESPN's Basketball Power Index predicts the Heat will finish the season with just 38 wins. That's already down from 46 projected wins in the preseason, and just one ahead of this historical franchise benchmark. Ben Golliver: Overreaction Let's be clear: The Antetokounmpo era in South Beach is off to an atrocious start. Instead of building off its blockbuster trade for the two-time MVP with a transformative offseason, the Heat lost Norman Powell to the Chicago Bulls in free agency and settled for adding Klay Thompson , who is a shell of his former self at age 36. On the court, it's already clear that the Heat need another proven ball handler and more shooting, and Antetokounmpo needs more time to jell with Bam Adebayo . Despite all those challenges, it's reasonable to give Heat coach Erik Spoelstra and his staff a long runway . Antetokounmpo's need to dominate the ball has clashed with the free-flowing offensive system that Miami utilized in 2025-26, and several veteran players seem to be easing into the new season. Spoelstra is a tinkerer who has conjured winning records from less talented rosters, and he'll be willing to trust his younger options if Miami's offensive struggles persist. It's probably best to withhold judgment until after the Heat's upcoming trip out West. If the Heat can't get right against teams such as the LA Clippers , Sacramento Kings , Golden State Warriors and Utah Jazz , sound the alarm. There is some good news: Antetokounmpo has been very productive in the early going, averaging 27.6 points, 11.2 rebounds and 4.6 assists after missing most of last season due to injuries. The Oklahoma City Thunder 's title hopes are gone without Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace . Kram: Not an overreaction Earlier this week, I went into more depth about the impact of these two long-term injuries on Oklahoma City's title chances. The simplified version: The Thunder's winning formula over the past few seasons has been to combine MVP-level offense from Gilgeous-Alexander with the best defense in the league. The collective loss of Williams, Wallace and Luguentz Dort (via summer trade) bends that second factor out of shape. Yes, centers Chet Holmgren and Isaiah Hartenstein still form an imposing backline, and Alex Caruso (currently out with an ankle sprain ) remains a singular defensive force. But the rest of Oklahoma City's perimeter rotation is now so thin, with enough defensive questions, that I would be surprised if it won another title -- barring a return from one of those injured starters before the playoffs or a significant in-season trade. Golliver: (emotional) overreaction Yes, it sure felt as if the sky was falling Monday when Thunder general manager Sam Presti announced that Williams and Wallace are out for the foreseeable future with significant injuries . That's no way to launch a title chase. After those injuries and the offseason trades of Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe , the Thunder are down five of their top six players by minutes logged during the 2024-25 championship season. Oof. But there's an awful lot of talent remaining around Gilgeous-Alexander, who has been sensational to start this season. Oklahoma City showed its resolve by beating Phoenix on Monday night, and it's worth noting it was only one win from reaching the Finals last year despite an injury-plagued season and postseason for Williams. Presti has picks and tradeable contracts to invest in stop-gap additions before the trade deadline, but he also has a deep roster that was built for the long haul. Count out the Thunder at your own peril. Ty Jerome will be an All-Star. Golliver: Overreaction Only a jerk would root against Jerome, who looks destined for a career year after surviving countless fits and starts to get here. But the Memphis Grizzlies ' schedule has been about as soft as it gets to start the season: The Jazz look poised to give up 30 points to any opposing guard, while the Warriors' injury issues and the Kings' general dysfunction disqualify them from being quality wins. Jerome is a talented scorer who more than earned this promotion to lead ball handler, but let's check back in a few weeks. The good news: LeBron James and Kawhi Leonard left the Western Conference over the summer, so there are more available All-Star spots than usual. Kram: Not an overreaction Jerome wasn't an All-Star last season, of course, because he played only 15 games. But he has been a star-level offensive player for a while now, even if few people recognized it until he started averaging 30 points. Here are the NBA's leaders in offensive box plus-minus for the 2025-26 campaign: Nikola Jokic Shai Gilgeous-Alexander Ty Jerome Luka Doncic Giannis Antetokounmpo Kawhi Leonard Victor Wembanyama Stephen Curry Jamal Murray Donovan Mitchell It doesn't matter when Jimmy Butler III returns -- the Golden State Warriors are cooked. Golliver: Not an overreaction The Warriors finally got their first win of the season Monday, but their opening week has been disheartening. With Butler, Kristaps Porzingis and several players missing time with injuries or ailments, the Warriors sat Curry on a back-to-back and rolled out a starting lineup featuring Yaxel Lendeborg , Brandon Williams , Will Richard , Gui Santos and Graham Ike on Saturday against the Phoenix Suns . That five-man group -- great fodder for Charles Barkley on "Who he play for?" -- will combine to earn less than $20 million this season. Meanwhile, Butler ($56 million) and Porzingis ($19.5 million) are missing in action. There's no way to overcome that math. Kram: Not an overreaction We finally agree, Ben. I'm not especially surprised by the Warriors' predicament because this seemed like a gap year from the start, due to all their injury issues and the lack of any real upgrades over the summer. (Aside from Lendeborg, who looks incredible as a rookie.) Maybe they can stick around the play-in race because the West looks shallower than usual -- the Jazz might also be cooked if Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr . are out for a while -- but Golden State's most important goal should be setting itself up for greater success in 2027-28. The San Antonio Spurs will kill their three-guard starting lineup by Thanksgiving. Kram: Overreaction I tend to think debates about starting lineups are overblown because of how much teams mix and match over the course of a game; lo and behold, the guard trio of De'Aaron Fox , Dylan Harper and Stephon Castle has shared the court for just 43 minutes across four games this season. And while it's way too early to come to significant conclusions using net rating, it's not as if the Spurs have struggled in those minutes. They're plus-15.4 with that three-guard lineup, according to databallr. If San Antonio's coaching staff believes it needs to keep Fox, Harper and Castle in the starting lineup for intangible reasons, then there's no evidence yet that that's a bad idea. Golliver: Overreaction Spurs coach Mitch Johnson could be headed for a real saga that might take months to play out. Of course, the critical decision is whether to start Fox, Harper or both point guards. But Johnson could also buy time for that duo to work things out by swapping Devin Vassell for Tobias Harris or Julian Champagnie . Given Fox's enormous salary and Harper's potential, San Antonio must exhaust every possibility before shifting one guard to the bench. Sacramento Kings coach Doug Christie won't make it to the new year. Golliver: Not an overreaction There are so many red flags coming out of Sacramento that it's starting to look like an Olympics opening ceremony. Naturally, the central tension concerns rookie guard Darius Acuff Jr . and veterans Domantas Sabonis and Zach LaVine . The Kings have turned Acuff loose for 93(!) shots in his first four career games with hopes he will develop into a franchise guard, but his more experienced teammates have good reason to wonder whether that's the best approach to winning. Christie is stuck, and Ben Simmons ' preseason Achilles tear made a tough job even tougher. The Kings look destined to be the NBA's worst team, and that level of ineptitude typically prompts a response from owner Vivek Ranadivé. Kram: Not an overreaction The Kings have let go of five coaches since Ranadivé bought the team in 2013. Two firings came at the end of a season (George Karl in 2016 and Dave Joerger in 2019), but the other three came early in a campaign: Luke Walton (2021) in November and Michael Malone (2014) and Mike Brown (2024) in December. That pattern tells me there's greater than a 50% chance that Christie won't make it to 2027. The New York Knicks won't get out of the first round. Kram: Overreaction I predicted before the season that New York would win fewer regular-season games than a year ago, so I can't profess to be surprised by their sub-.500 start against a tough schedule. The greatest on-court problem for the Knicks is their 25th-ranked offense, but I expect a prompt turnaround: They rank last in making just 30% of their midrange shots, per Cleaning the Glass, after ranking fifth at 45% with largely the same roster a year ago. In looking ahead to the postseason, moreover, I would have to see a much larger sample of struggles to consider the likelihood that New York won't be favored in any playoff matchup in the East. The competition will be tougher this year, but the Knicks are proven playoff performers. Golliver: Not an overreaction This one is more about vibes than hard analytics. As is often the case for defending champions, the Knicks have had a challenging opening week schedule filled with marquee opponents. In that context, the 2-3 start really isn't the end of the world. New York was in competitive games against aspiring contenders in the 76ers and Celtics last week and then handed the Detroit Pistons their first loss on Tuesday. But the Knicks' inability to pull out those close games was a reminder of just how charmed their 2026 postseason was from start to finish. Jalen Brunson seemingly hit every big shot he needed to hit, and the one time Brunson didn't come through, OG Anunoby was right there for the one-in-a-million tip-in. Time after time, the Knicks cheated death with second-half comebacks. That doesn't feel like a sustainable formula now that they've got the target on their backs. Owner James Dolan has also operated like a man who is comfortable with one ring rather than desperate to add another. Trying to win back-to-back championships has exhausted younger teams than the Knicks in recent years, so no one should be all that surprised if they run out of gas or encounter season-altering injuries before May. Offseason trades made the Charlotte Hornets ' current roster better . Kram: Not an overreaction (although I'm prepared for Ball to make this statement look silly) We all thought Charlotte's surprising offseason trades were made with an eye toward the future. After all, the franchise dealt two foundational players and their two highest-salaried players in Ball and Miles Bridges . But the Hornets received so much flexibility and so many valuable draft assets in return that the "one step back, two steps forward" approach made sense. We might have been giving the Hornets' present-day roster short shrift with that assessment. Charlotte has a winning record despite receiving zero minutes from its starting backcourt, as Coby White and Kon Knueppel deal with injuries. Brandon Miller appears to have taken a leap after signing a five-year rookie extension. And offseason additions Naz Reid and Grayson Allen , who came to Charlotte as part of the Ball and Bridges trades, have combined to average 36.3 points while making 44% of their 3-pointers. Reid, in particular, represents a meaningful upgrade over Bridges at power forward. Golliver: Overreaction The jury is still out on the Hornets given the injuries you mentioned and their weak quality of competition to date. With that said, the decision to trade Bridges is already shaping up to be one of those moves they will never regret. Charlotte's short-term success will be determined by Miller's ability to consistently flex his muscles as an alpha scorer and Knueppel's comfort handling greater playmaking duties. Beyond that, Hornets ownership must demonstrate a willingness to spend to build around that budding duo. The Ball trade could wind up as a win-win for Charlotte and Minnesota, but at some point, the Hornets will need to prioritize talent acquisition and retention rather than careful cap management. Otherwise, they're spinning their wheels. Walker Kessler should be on Team USA in 2028. Golliver: Not an overreaction Before the season, the Lakers argued that Kessler was worth paying a premium price in draft picks in their summer sign-and-trade with the Jazz because it's incredibly difficult to find centers at his age (25) with the ability to finish plays on offense and credibly protect the paint on defense. Grant Hill, Spoelstra and USA Basketball would be wise to target big men with that exact skill set for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, especially if Joel Embiid , Anthony Davis and James opt not to return after winning gold in Paris. Adebayo, Holmgren, Jackson and Evan Mobley could all be in the mix, but Kessler brings a level of sheer size and physicality that those players lack. Wouldn't it be helpful to have a traditional center to deploy with Wembanyama and Jokic looming as threats to the U.S. dynasty? Kram: Overreaction You cited the Grizzlies' schedule when cautioning about Jerome's hot start. I'll do the same for Kessler, whose two big games to date came against a Warriors team that didn't start a center and a Clippers team with Isaiah Jackson in the middle. That's not exactly Wembanyama- and Jokic-level competition. Kessler does have international experience, as he was a deep reserve for the unsuccessful 2023 World Cup squad. I believe he's on the long list of American big men for 2028, but I would need much more evidence to place him higher in the pecking order. The Chicago Bulls will be the worst team in the East. Golliver: Not an overreaction For all the preseason talk about improved parity this season thanks to the new lottery rules , there are still some pretty bad teams. The Bulls, Bucks and Nets have all looked like viable contenders to finish with the conference's worst record. (And yet, somehow, the Heat have been harder to watch than all of them.) The scary part about Chicago's start is how thoroughly Toronto and Boston thumped the Bulls. While the Bulls want to play fast under new coach Tiago Splitter, they're just getting completely run off the court by good teams. There's obviously no reason to panic if the blowout losses mount: Caleb Wilson should be encouraged to play free and make mistakes, and Chicago's new front office should focus on which of its veteran players look like long-term fits around the promising rookie forward. And is it too early to predict the Bulls will be getting rid of players at the trade deadline? Kram: Overreaction The Bulls rank dead last in offensive efficiency, but I believe that's more a product of bad luck than bad process. According to GeniusIQ tracking, the Bulls rank fourth in quantified shot probability, which accounts for factors such as location, defender distance and shooter talent. But the Bulls have underperformed that shot quality by 11.1%, which ranks last by a mile. For context, the largest gap for any team over the full 2025-26 season was just 1.7% -- so Chicago's shotmaking is bound to improve. That doesn't mean I think the Bulls will reach the play-in tournament or anything so lofty. But I do believe that they'll play more like a typical rebuilding team going forward, rather than losing every other game by blowout margins.

NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Alex Goodlett/Getty Images) | Getty Images “Are they going to put Wemby back in?” It was an excellent question, and one that I had myself. It was, in a way, the question of the season so far when it comes to a Spurs team that has scuffled quite a bit coming out of the gate. The starting unit, forced into a new configuration by the ascension of the prodigious Dylan Harper, has looked disjointed and seems to do its scoring in fits and starts. The bench, on the other hand, seems almost lost — unmoored without the steady hand of the rookie who led it for most of last season. The one player holding everything together has been, somewhat predictably, Wembanyama, and the better part of almost every game has seemed to hinge on his presence and the antigravity of his occasional absence. But, to paraphrase an episode of Cartoon Network’s Samurai Jack , even the gods must rest, and for all his gifts, Wemby is not a god. With nine minutes left in a game that the shorthanded Utah Jazz had spent clawing for every point, Mitch Johnson had made the call to give Wemby a quick breather. That seemed reasonable. Wemby would catch his breath and then jump right back in, right? Right? The Spurs were clinging to a six point lead when Wemby headed for the sideline, and Spurs Twitter was awash with (understandable) anxiety. The Spurs had trailed for most of the first half and had finally clawed their way to a lead, but it was a tenuous bargain with a scoreboard that seemed determined to forsake its oath to the Silver and Black. In fact, I was beginning to doubt its fealty altogether. With every Wemby exit, betrayal was in the air, and San Antonio’s 2nd unit (and Luke Kornet in particular) were bearing the brunt of the Jazz’s unholy pact with the jumbotron. Utah had shot nearly 60% from the field in the 3rd quarter, and it felt like they were heating up again. Everything seemed to be going in. The post was a turnstile. The rim was actively thwarting San Antonio’s short-armed stabs at conversion. It was getting dramatic. Catastrophic, even. You’d be forgiven for thinking that the atmosphere more closely resembled that of a postseason contest rather than game 5 of 82, on a Wednesday night in late October. I’m not ashamed to say that I got caught up in it a little myself. When you’re an avid fan of a sports team, there’s this bizarre and inexplicable fusion that occurs. It’s not quite empathy per se, but an identification that spans the gap between the professionals on the court and the plebeians on the couch. You get to feel an echo of their joy and the spectre of their pain. Their wins make you hopeful for your own, but their losses can do the inverse. It’s silly, and strange, and wonderfully human. And somehow, it allows for a communion between disparate individuals that feels like alchemy — a group connection that pulls you into a maelstrom of emotion and connection. It’s damn near irresistible, which is probably why I found myself loudly bemoaning the appearance of Kornet as Wemby trotted off, in spite of my long-standing fondness for The Big Elote. And to be fair, Kornet’s been a shadow of his 2025-26 self, carrying with him the play that (unfortunately) defined San Antonio’s big-man deficit in the NBA Finals. I’m not sure it’s a playoff hangover, or a crisis of confidence, or a small nagging injury of some sort, but the Kornet of the Western Conference Finals has yet to be seen, and, as a fellow Spurs fan pointed out , the Spurs have been hemorrhaging points during his limited stints. Within a minute, the game was tied again. Devin Vassell (who had been cold most of the night) and Stephon Castle were doing their best to keep things from getting ugly on the offensive end, keeping pace with a Jazz team that clearly smelled blood. With six-and-a-half minutes left in the game, Will Hardy called a timeout. Finally, a break! Mitch could substitute Wemby in without using a valuable timeout of his own. And without hesitation, he subbed Keldon Johnson in for Julian Champagnie, the Spurs’ best three-point shooter. What?? The confusion was widespread. What about Wemby? What about the lead? “Are they going to put Wemby back in?” my daughter inquired from her end of the couch. She really only recognizes three players: Devin (my name), Fox (a favorite animal), and Wemby, but having retired from her coloring book for the evening, she was now peppering me with questions as she crawled over to lean against my knees. “Yeah, they’re gonna put Wemby in real soon.” Ten seconds later San Antonio’s skipper called a timeout of his own. Oh. I guess it was just a mistake. Not ideal, but not costly, I guess. No substitution at all? I could hear the consternation as if I were within the confines of a fan section at the Frost Bank Center. I had to bottle up any profanity for the sake of the five-year-old lounging against my knees, but I was silently livid. And my daughter, attuned to adult emotion in that way that we don’t give children enough credit for, cheerily reassured me. “It’s okay, I see Devin,” she said as she patted my leg consolingly. Almost as if on cue, Vassell sunk a 20-footer in the face of the defense. About time, I thought to myself. But Vassell had been shooting better for most of the quarter, even if I had failed to notice. “See!” she said elatedly, displaying the kind of childlike credulity that gospels allude to. Little did either of us know that her three favorite players were about to take us on a magic carpet ride out of danger and into the win column. Vassell hit two more shots on passes from Wemby, which proved (along with a tip-in from Keldon and a buzzer-beating miss from Fox) to be just enough to get the Spurs to overtime. And it was there that Vassell and Co. picked up right where they left off, with all but two of San Antonio’s points scored or assisted on by Devin, Fox, and Wemby. The icing on the cake was a steal and a racing dunk from Fox with less than a minute left. Its parallel as an opposite to his endlessly replayed hesitation in the Finals wasn’t lost on me. “I told you it would be okay.” “You were right. I guess I should listen to you more.” “Yeah, you should.” I think Billy Joel has a song about women always being women at every phase of life, or something like that. No argument here, though. I’ve got a lot of childlike believing to do if I want to enter the kingdom of heaven. How much do I have to have for another Finals win, though? I guess we’ll find out. It’s a new dawn, it’s a new day, it’s a Nina Simone song. I think I’ll take the win while I can. Takeaways I don’t think it’s a coincidence that both Kornet and Keldon have had such a rough/inconsistent start to the season, with Harper spending so much time with the starters. Yes, Mitch has made sure to keep at least one of the star guards on when the bench takes their turn, but that’s not the same thing as the consistency that the 2nd unit experienced with Harper running it. Hopefully, Harper will get more time with the bench once Tobias Harris returns from injury (though the starting unit will then have to adapt to that), as both Keldon and Kornet benefited greatly from his presence; if not, I think it would be ideal to at least use one of the guards consistently with the 2nd unit, so that they can build a rhythm and rapport. Last year Kornet was the only real option as a backup for Wemby, but the San Antonio braintrust might want to consider giving Tarris Reed some run on nights that Kornet doesn’t seem to have it. Of course, it’s possible that the bench will continue having issues until the guard issue is somewhat resolved. But hey, why not give it the old college try? He might be a rookie, but Reed has a serious motor, and some considerable heft. If nothing else, the change of pace might come in handy when a team is making easy work of Kornet’s defensive efforts. It’s early yet, but two things are beginning to stick out as minor trends: 1. The Spurs have really cracked down on sloppy mistakes, as they’re leading the league in fewest turnovers per game right now. 2. They just can’t seem to get to the line, as they’re the 4th-lowest team in free-throw attempts and have the 3rd-lowest free-throw rate. The first thing is really good, and evidence that the offensive flow feels a bit worse than it is. But the second thing might serve as proof that the lack of spacing is really hurting San Antonio’s ability to drive to the hoop, something that served as a meal ticket last season when shots weren’t falling. The three-guard experiment is a bit of a mixed bag so far, so let’s hope they either figure it out soon or make a change to loosen things up. However, in spite of those issues, it’s important to note that the Spurs are still 5th in the NBA in points scored in the paint. That’s because, for the past two games (and most of the season), Wemby has been shoving the ball down the throats of anyone bold enough to meet him around the rim. And when his outside shot is on, as it was last night, he’s nigh unstoppable. Poor Jaxson Hayes looked like he didn’t know whether he was coming or going after two quarters of that. It seems like Wemby’s really dedicated himself to interior scoring this year, and frankly, it’s terrifying. Playing You Out – The Theme Song of the Evening: Feeling Good by Nina Simone

teamStories.detailText: On Tuesday, Julian Champagnie came into the Spurs game against the Sacramento Kings and dropped eight three-pointers in thirteen minutes, tying his own franchise record. He dropped eight in the first half against the New York Knicks on New Year’s Eve last year, then came back in the second half and hit three more. Through my Spurs-colored glasses, Champagnie looks to be one of the best in the league. But this Venn Diagram I found through StatMuse lays it out clearly. Julian Champagnie. pic.twitter.com/VWINJaCDlW — StatMuse (@statmuse) October 28, 2026 Of current NBA players, Champagnie is one of seven players who tally 3+ made three-pointers per game while shooting at 45% or better. Here’s the kicker — Julian isn’t succeeding solely on offense, he is also one of twenty-two players who are recording three or more “stocks” per game. “Stocks” is a portmanteau for steals and blocks. In other words, Champagnie is killing it on both ends of the court. His shooting benefits from the attention given to Victor Wembanyama. At any time, Wemby is being doubled, leaving an open man. Champagnie is often that lone man, and he has found that he can hit from anywhere beyond the arc. When he gets hot…watch out. Defensively speaking, Julian is sneaky, quick, and agile. His athleticism allows him to get to pull boards, often times against larger opponents. He is the 3-and-D guy that the Spurs needed to expose weaknesses in opposition. When you put the three-point shooting prowess in the diagram with the stocks, Champagnie is in a category all his own. A one-man wolf pack , if you will. Unfortunately, the T-wolves are without Anthony Edwards for the next couple of months as he tends to his right knee. It is an unfortunate turn for Minnesota who just brought in LaMelo Ball to partner with Edwards. There have been a rash of early season injuries plaguing the league. teamStories.title: Harrison Barnes not spooked by Spurs' start, speaks on giving back with UNICEF
teamStories.summary: The San Antonio Spurs lost their first two games, but Harrison Barnes isn't spooked. Here's his thoughts on the season, Victor Wembanyama and working with UNICEF.
teamStories.detailText: Losing the first two games of the NBA season might cause a scare. But the San Antonio Spurs weren't fazed when they did so this month and rebounded with two straight wins. Veteran forward Harrison Barnes explained the mindset that the defending Western Conference champions are carrying in the 2026-27 campaign. "Every day, we kind of pursue a standard, and I think to start the season, we were able to look around the locker room and say that we weren't at the standard that we wanted to play at," he told USA TODAY Sports in an interview on behalf of UNICEF. "So I think for us, it's just a matter of can we go out every single night and be happy with the product that we put on the floor?" Brushing off the fright of the early season, Barnes, 34, wants people to embrace a not-so-spooky Halloween tradition: Trick-or-Treat with UNICEF. He is a spokesman for the organization's 76-year program, which he participated in as a kid. The little orange cardboard box that kids take with them to not only ask for candy, but for cash to help underprivileged children, creates a sense of nostalgia for the veteran forward. "UNICEF is an organization that I know very well," he said. "This Trick-or-Treat for UNICEF is something that I did as a kid, and I truly believe that it's important to give back and to bring awareness to children that are in need." View this post on Instagram Barnes has fond memories of trick-or-treating with his younger sister, Jourdan-Ashle Barnes, and comparing whose candy haul was better. He now shares the joy of Halloween with his daughter, who Barnes says enjoys dressing up as characters from "Frozen," "Moana" and "Encanto." "It was always something that was fun for us," he said. "And you know, as a father, you want to pass on some of those same values to your children." When he was a member of the Dallas Mavericks back in 2018, Barnes credited his mother, Shirley, for teaching him the importance of helping others. She experienced homelessness when Barnes was a baby and, when her children were older, they assisted in organizing clothes for her charity, Suited For Work Clothing Closet. "When you look at how all of us got here, it was a healthy foundation. It took a village, right?" he said. "It took a lot of people investing in our futures. And I think that having an equitable start at the beginning of a child's life obviously gives them the most potential to achieve anything that they want to achieve." Families can order their Trick-or-Treat for UNICEF boxes online and then donate the proceeds from Halloween via CoinStar, credit card or check. The organization was also responsible for the photo shoot where Lionel Messi gave a baby Lamine Yamal a bath . The image served as a wink of destiny as Yamal's Spain beat Messi's Argentina in this summer's World Cup final . Besides being a leader for his family and in the community, Barnes signed a one-year contract extension over the summer to continue his role as a mentor for the Spurs. He won the 2015 NBA championship as a member of the Golden State Warriors and is in his third year with San Antonio, calling the deal "an unbelievable opportunity." "The biggest thing I can lend is my voice, my experience, just in terms of trying to be a little bit of just emotional stability for the group," he said. "Obviously, we have so much talent on our roster that I think it's always important just to kind of stay level-headed. And hopefully, if we continue to do that, like I said, and stick to the things we know to be true on the floor, I think we'll put ourselves in a good position most nights." The star of San Antonio that has the basketball world on high alert is Victor Wembanyama. The 22-year-old was the Defensive Player of the Year last season and set a blocks record in the playoffs . In USA TODAY's preseason ranking of the top 100 players in the league, Wembanyama is No. 3. Barnes shared what he thinks makes the French sensation stand out. "Victor's great. He's one of my closest friends on the team," he said. "I think the thing that makes him an unbelievable basketball player, but also just a great person in general is that he's a constant learner, and he has an extreme curiosity of how to improve himself. "I think he finds ways on and off the court to just grow, develop, talk to people, get experiences, learn. I think that's what's allowed him to be on the trajectory that he's on right now."
